title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: It was almost three o'clock and nobody had gone to sleep yet when the quartermaster turned up with an order to move on to the little town of Ostrovna. The officers, still laughing and talking, began packing in a hurry and boiled up some more muddy water in the samovar. Rostov didn't wait for tea but went off to his squadron. Day was breaking, the rain had stopped and the clouds were thinning out. It was damp and cold, especially in clothes that hadn't dried. As they came out of the tavern into the half-light of dawn, Rostov and Ilyin both glanced under the wet, shining leather hood of the doctor's cart. His feet stuck out from under the apron, and in the middle of it they could see his wife's nightcap and hear her sleepy breathing.
"She really is a dear little thing," Rostov said to Ilyin, who was riding behind him.
"A charming woman!" said Ilyin, with all the seriousness of a sixteen-year-old boy.

Half an hour later the squadron stood drawn up on the road. The command "Mount!" rang out, and the soldiers crossed themselves and got into the saddle. Rostov, riding in front, called "Forward!" and the hussars moved off in files of four along the broad road lined with birch trees on both sides. Their sabers clanked, they talked in low voices, and their horses' hoofs splashed in the mud. They followed the infantry and a battery that had gone ahead.

Torn, blue-purple clouds, turning red in the east, raced before the wind. It kept getting lighter. The curly grass that always grows along country roads came into clear view, still wet from the night's rain. The drooping branches of the birches, wet too, swayed in the wind and shook bright drops of water off to one side. The soldiers' faces grew clearer and clearer. Rostov rode along the edge of the road between the two rows of birches, with Ilyin always close behind him.

On campaign Rostov allowed himself the luxury of riding a Cossack horse instead of a regimental one. He was a connoisseur of horses and a keen sportsman, and he had recently got himself a big, handsome, spirited Don horse, dun-colored with a light mane and tail. When he rode it, no one could outgallop him. He enjoyed riding this horse, and he thought about the horse, about the morning, about the doctor's wife — and not once about the danger ahead.

In the past Rostov had been afraid when going into action; now he felt no fear at all. He was fearless, not because he had got used to being under fire (one can't get used to danger), but because he had learned to control his thoughts in the face of it. When going into action he had trained himself to think about anything except the very thing that might have seemed most likely to occupy him: the danger ahead. In his first period of service he had tried hard and reproached himself for cowardice, but he hadn't been able to do it; with time it had come on its own. Now he rode beside Ilyin under the birches, now and then pulling leaves off a branch within reach, sometimes touching his horse's side with his foot, or handing a finished pipe back to a hussar behind him without turning around. He did it all as calmly and carelessly as if he were just out for a ride. He looked with pity at Ilyin's excited face, for Ilyin talked a great deal and was in a state of great agitation. Rostov knew from experience the tormenting expectation of terror and death that the cornet was going through, and he knew that only time could help him.

As soon as the sun appeared in a clear strip of sky below the clouds, the wind dropped, as if it didn't dare spoil the beauty of the summer morning after the storm. Drops were still falling, but straight down now, and everything was quiet. The whole sun came up on the horizon and then vanished behind a long, narrow cloud that hung above it. A few minutes later it showed again, brighter, over the top of the cloud, tearing the cloud's edge. Everything grew bright and sparkled. And with that light, as if in answer to it, came the sound of guns ahead of them.
Rostov hadn't had time to think about how far off the firing was before Count Ostermann-Tolstoy's adjutant came galloping from Vitebsk with orders to advance at a trot along the road.

The squadron overtook and passed the infantry and the battery, which had also picked up speed. It rode down a hill, went through an empty, deserted village, and climbed again. The horses began to lather and the men to flush.
"Halt! Dress your ranks!" came the order of the regimental commander from ahead. "Forward by the left. Walk, march!" came the order from the front.

The hussars moved along the line of troops on the left flank of our position and halted behind our Uhlans, who were in the front line. To the right stood our infantry in a dense column; they were the reserve. Higher up the hill, right on the horizon, our guns could be seen through the wonderfully clear air, brightly lit by the slanting morning sun. Ahead, beyond a hollow valley, were the enemy's columns and guns. Our advanced line was already in action, and we could hear it exchanging brisk fire with the enemy in the valley.

At these sounds, which he hadn't heard for so long, Rostov's spirits rose as they would at the liveliest music. Trap-ta-ta-tap! the shots cracked, sometimes together, sometimes several in quick succession. Then all was silent again, and then again it sounded as if someone were walking on detonators and setting them off.

The hussars stayed where they were for about an hour. A cannonade started. Count Ostermann rode up behind the squadron with his suite, stopped, spoke to the regimental commander, and then rode on up the hill to the guns.
After Ostermann had gone, a command rang out to the Uhlans.

The infantry in front of them split into platoons to let the cavalry through. The Uhlans set off, the streamers on their lances fluttering, and trotted downhill toward the French cavalry, which could be seen below and to the left.

The moment the Uhlans were down the hill, the hussars were ordered up it to support the battery. As they took the places the Uhlans had left, bullets came from the front, whining and whistling, but they fell spent and did no harm.

These sounds, which he hadn't heard for so long, gave Rostov even more pleasure and excitement than the earlier firing had. He drew himself up and looked at the field of battle opening out below him from the hill, and with his whole soul he followed the movement of the Uhlans. They swept down close to the French dragoons, something confused happened there in the smoke, and five minutes later our Uhlans were galloping back, not to the place they had held but farther to the left. Among the orange-colored Uhlans on chestnut horses, and behind them in a large group, could be seen blue French dragoons on gray horses.
